description_full: CGI Inc. provides information technology and business process services in Western and Southern Europe, the United States, Canada, Scandinavia, Northwest and Central-East Europe, the United Kingdom, Australia, Germany, Finland, Poland, Baltics, and the Asia Pacific. It offers end-to-end services and solutions, including business and strategic IT consulting; systems integration, such as data integration, AI and automation integration, cloud integration, Internet of Things, enterprise application integration, application programming interface integration, and legacy system modernization; managed IT and business process; and application services comprising application management, DevSecOps, application modernization and rationalization, and quality engineering and assurance. The company also provides infrastructure services, which include legacy infrastructure modernization, cloud and hybrid infrastructure management, AI-powered IT service management, FinOps-enabled cloud management, cyber resilience and compliance, site reliability engineering and AIOps, and infrastructure-as-code; and intellectual property business solutions. It serves banking and capital markets, communications and media, energy and utilities, government, health, insurance, life sciences, manufacturing, retail and consumer services, space, transportation, and logistics industries. The company was formerly known as CGI Group Inc. and changed its name to CGI Inc. in January 2019. CGI Inc. was founded in 1976 and is headquartered in Montreal, Canada.

financial_summary: CGI Inc. is a large-cap technology business with a $16.7B market cap on $10.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 18% against a 8% cost of capital, a 10-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $1.5B in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.30× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 26× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 0.5%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Goodwill represents 57% of total assets — a large impairment risk hanging over book value
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Piotroski score 4/9 — below the median for a healthy business
Technology sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 7% over 3 months
Elevated sector volatility (38% annualized) adds uncertainty
Antitrust and platform-regulation risk — the larger the network effect, the larger the regulatory target on its back, and a single consent decree can reset the moat.
AI disruption of existing software moats — incumbents with durable margins face commoditisation as AI-native competitors replicate features at a fraction of the R&D cost.
Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 9% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Trading at a 75% margin of safety to estimated fair value — a real cushion against errors in the estimate
Market is pricing in lower growth than the company has historically delivered
Valued at a 59% discount to sector median EV/EBITDA
Returns on capital have been remarkably steady for 5 years — durability is the real test of a moat
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 16% operating margin runs 9pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.69x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-5.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 17% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 10% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 14% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 31% and a beta of 0.65, it is more defensive than the market.
About $31.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 46% in the 2020 crash, 17% in the 2022 bear market and 44% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 75% below its DCF fair value of $330, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 13%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $230 to $496 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 13.2 vs 27.4, EV/EBITDA 7.0 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 10.8 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 23% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 9.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 3 covering analysts target $86.03 on average, 5% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 18% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.12).
It converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.30x.
ROE of 18% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.5x net debt to EBITDA ($1.1B of cash against $2.0B of debt), with interest covered 26.2x.
Goodwill makes up 57% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.0% over 3 years and 3.4% over 5 years.
Free cash flow has compounded 6.8% a year over five years.
Analysts expect 18.1% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and institutions hold 72%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.5% (0.6% in dividends).
people: With about 94,000 employees, each generates about $115K of revenue, 0.3x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 3.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $16K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $954K (8x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
